extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of poetic craft (readers of classical Latin/Greek models)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and aesthetic rules for composing poetry and plays: unity, diction, metre, dramatic propriety, chorus and music, revision, and the moral/technical qualities expected of a poet. Grounded in Horace's Ars Poetica and aimed at authors and students seeking classical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem demands unity, to be secured by harmony and proportion, as well as a wise choice of subject and good diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the work cohesive and proportioned; avoid unrelated embellishments. The whole piece should present an artistic unity (Ars Poetica 1-23). Anti-patterns: disjointed elements that break harmony or unnecessary complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate metre and style to theme and character
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre and style must be appropriate to theme and to character; tone and style should suit the kind of verse or dramatic personae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match rhythm and diction to the subject and to the characters speaking (e.g., tragic vs. comic speech). Wrong: mixing lofty diction with low characters or putting comic language into tragic scenes (ll. 73-118).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confine to subjects within your power
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer should confine himself to subjects within his power so he will not be at a loss for words and will follow a correct order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select material you can handle convincingly; this promotes coherence and correct sequencing. Anti-pattern: attempting grand subjects beyond skill and losing control of the narrative (38-45).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fresh diction and moderate invention of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful in choice of language; by skilful combination you can freshen familiar terms and may coin words in moderation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovate sparingly — moderate neologisms are permissible (46-72). Avoid gratuitous coinages or forced archaisms that jar the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow tried Greek models (especially Homer) for metre and form
rubrics_metrics.description: The metres most fitting for the several types of verse were established by great Greek poets; a good model will always be found in Homer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study Greek models day and night to learn appropriate rhythms and forms; imitation of well-tested models is recommended for quality (73-85, repeated elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character drawing and propriety of representation in drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic poetry requires special care in character portrayal and propriety of representation; famous/homeric characters must be depicted as tradition expects, new characters must be internally consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure characters act and speak in ways true to their nature or to established literary tradition; inconsistency or improper portrayal yields ridicule (119-127, 153-178). Example: Achilles, Medea, Orestes should comport with their known traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play structure: five acts
rubrics_metrics.description: A play should be in five acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to a five-act structure as the normative dramatic form (189-192). This is guidance for classical dramatic proportion and pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use deus ex machina only rarely
rubrics_metrics.description: The deus ex machina should be employed only rarely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid convenient supernatural resolutions except when truly warranted—overuse undermines dramatic credibility (189-192).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit number of characters on stage
rubrics_metrics.description: There should never be more than three characters on the stage at one time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep scenes focused and manageable; too many simultaneous characters dilute clarity and stage effect (189-192).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus must have a real part and moral purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should take a real part in the action; it should not sing anything irrelevant, and should promote the cause of morality and religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the chorus advances plot or theme, supports moral aims, and avoids irrelevant or purely decorative song (193-201). Anti-pattern: a chorus that sings off-topic pieces or merely fills time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music and instrumentation proportionate to theatre and taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Music (e.g., flute) once accompanied the chorus simply; with luxury music became florid and sensational, corrupting taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use music to support the chorus without overpowering drama; avoid florid, sensational music that masks weak diction or panders to luxury (202-219).

rubrics_metrics.name: Satyric drama: balanced language between tragedy and comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Satyric drama should have a tone between tragic and comic: familiar but not coarse; rustic characters must not use city wits' language, nor should gods and heroes use vulgar speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a 'happy mean' in diction for satyr plays; avoid vulgarity for elevated figures and avoid giving rustic characters urbane affectations (220-250).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre: know measure function and avoid obscuring rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: The iambic is a rapid measure; a senarius counts as a trimeter. Older poets admitted spondees freely, which could obscure rhythm and make verse heavy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand metrical character (speed, weight) and avoid overuse of substitutions (e.g., excessive spondees) that destroy musicality. Study Greek models to recognize unmusical verses (251-274).

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise: subject every poem to the finishing touch
rubrics_metrics.description: Condemn every poem which has not been subjected to the finishing touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polish and finish before publishing; incomplete or unrefined poems are unworthy (285-294). Anti-pattern: hasty publication of unedited work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wisdom, study, and life-experience as prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: First essential is wisdom; study philosophers and life itself so personages will speak like real living beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate knowledge of human nature and practical wisdom; apply learned lessons to craft believable characters (309-322).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine utile with dulce (instruct and please)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry aims at both instruction and pleasure; combine usefulness with delight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In didactic passages be concise; in fiction avoid extravagance. Blending instruction and pleasure improves lasting appeal and commercial success (323-346).

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and practice are necessary (genius needs discipline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural ability alone is not enough; genius must be trained—like athletes—and practice is required for poetic achievement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop skill by study and discipline; do not rely on raw talent alone (408-418, 347-360). Anti-pattern: slovenly habits excused as 'genius'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit to impartial criticism and be ready to excise weak lines
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet should submit what he writes to a good critic and have the courage to remove words that lack dignity or weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the spirit of an honest censor; accept and profit from impartial evaluation (106-116, 361-390). Example: removing lines that 'are deemed unworthy of rank'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mediocrity; aim for high excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediocrity is never allowed in poetry whose aim is to give pleasure; slight defects can be tolerated but not mediocrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train diligently and avoid complacency; appreciate good lines even in poor poems but strive for overall high standard (347-360).

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin simply and omit what cannot be adorned
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a simple beginning (as Homer did), hurry on with narrative, and omit what you cannot adorn; never lose the thread of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clarity and forward motion over long, ornate introductions. Anti-pattern: overlong prefaces that stall the narrative (128-152).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use narrative vs. action appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Events may be set forth in action or, less preferably, in narrative; narrative should be used for revolting and incredible incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatize credible events; reserve narrative reporting for incidents that would strain credulity on stage (179-188).

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray traditional mythic figures faithfully but allow original handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Achilles, Medea, Orestes must be portrayed as known in Greek literature; yet in public (Homeric) property you may gain private rights by original handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect audience expectations for famous figures, but originality in treatment can create distinctive claims if consistent and plausible (119-127).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extremes and their opposites
rubrics_metrics.description: Guard against extremes, and while avoiding one error do not fall into its opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek balanced judgments; avoid overcorrections that produce other faults (24-31). Example: in style or ornamentation do not swing from excess to sterility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt language to the characters (propriety of speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: A play must appeal to feelings of an audience and language must be adapted to the characters impersonated; lack of agreement provokes scorn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor diction and tone to status, role, and situation of speakers. Anti-pattern: mismatched diction that makes characters laughable (86-118).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to detail without losing overall success
rubrics_metrics.description: Like a good sculptor or painter, pay attention to detail but ensure the work as a whole succeeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance careful workmanship on parts with the effect of the total work; avoid details that conflict with the whole (32-37).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using poetry at the expense of health or judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not worth composing poetry at the expense of your wits or health; genius-is-madness notion is taken too far.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not romanticize slovenly habits or madness; preserve health, common sense, and social duties while practicing the art (295-308, 438-452).
